procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court: Shah, J. of the Bombay High Court
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated August 10, 1961 of the Bombay High Court in Appeal No. 23 of 1960.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
Trial Court: Shah, J. held that the appellant was entitled to salary and allowances up to the date when he was dismissed i.e., February 11, 1960. He granted a declaration that the order of suspension was illegal and inoperative in law and the appellant continued to be on duty till February 11, 1960 as though no order of suspension had been made. He also granted a decree directing the respondent to pay to the appellant Rs. 51,135.28 with interest on Rs. 43,223/- at the rate of 4 per cent p.a. and the cost of the suit.

High Court (Appellate Bench): The respondent appealed against the judgment of the trial Judge. The Appellate Bench held that the respondent had inherent power to suspend the appellant and to withhold full remuneration for the period of suspension under Rule 151 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The Appellate Bench therefore held that the order of suspension made by the respondent was legally valid. The Appellate Bench also held that the suit was barred under Article 14 of the Schedule to the Indian Limitation Act. For these reasons the Appellate Bench allowed the appeal, set aside the decree passed by the trial Judge and dismissed the suit.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate from the judgment of the Bombay High Court dated August 10, 1961.

directions: set aside the decree passed by the trial Judge
ordered the appellant to pay four-fifths of the costs of the respondent throughout

issue.issue_text: Whether the power to suspend a public servant pending an inquiry into misconduct is an implied term in the contract of employment, or must it be expressly provided for by statute or the contract itself.

facts: A public servant (the appellant) was suspended pending an inquiry into his misconduct.

The appellant argued that the government had no power to suspend him because this power was not an express term in his contract of employment or in the relevant statutory rules (Bombay Civil Service Rules).
law: The Court distinguished between two types of suspension: (1) suspending the entire contract of service, and (2) suspending an employee from performing their duties while the contract remains subsisting.
The power to suspend the entire contract of service (where the employer is not bound to pay) must be expressly provided for in a statute or contract.
The power to suspend an employee from performing their duties is an implied term in every contract of service.
If an employee is suspended under this implied power, they are entitled to their full remuneration unless a specific statute or rule allows the employer to withhold or reduce it.
application: The Court applied the principle that the power to direct an employee not to work pending an inquiry is an inherent right of the employer, flowing from the subsisting employment contract.
The appellant's argument failed because it did not recognize this distinction. The government had the implied power to suspend him from his duties.
The question of the appellant's pay during the suspension period would then be a separate issue, determined by the applicable rules (like the Bombay Civil Service Rules).
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the power to suspend a public servant from performing their duties pending an inquiry is an implied term in the contract of employment, even if not expressly stated. However, the employee's right to remuneration during this period can only be withheld or modified if a specific statute or rule permits it.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of suspension pending an inquiry into a criminal charge automatically terminates upon the acquittal of the employee in the criminal proceedings.

facts: An employee was suspended by an order dated February 19, 1950.
The suspension order explicitly stated that the suspension was "pending further orders".
The employee was subsequently acquitted of the criminal charges by the High Court on February 15, 1952.
The employee argued that his acquittal automatically terminated the suspension order.
law: The termination of a suspension order is governed by the specific terms of that order.
A suspension order that is explicitly "pending further orders" does not terminate automatically but requires a subsequent, separate order to be lifted.
application: The Supreme Court examined the specific language of the suspension order in this case.
It found that the phrase "pending further orders" clearly indicated that the suspension was not self-terminating upon the conclusion of the criminal proceedings.
The Court reasoned that for the suspension to end, the government needed to issue a "further order" explicitly terminating it.

The Court also distinguished a case cited by the appellant (from the Orissa High Court) by noting that the suspension order in that case did not contain the phrase "pending further orders" and was issued under a specific rule linking suspension to the duration of criminal proceedings, which was not the situation here.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the order of suspension did not automatically terminate upon the employee's acquittal. Because the order was made "pending further orders," it remained in effect until the government issued a separate order to terminate it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power to suspend a public servant pending an inquiry into misconduct is an implied term in the contract of employment, or must it be expressly provided for by statute or the contract itself.
appellant_arguments: The power to suspend an employee must be expressly provided for by statute or the contract of employment and cannot be an implied term. (inferred)
respondent_arguments: The power to suspend the appellant was expressly provided for under Rules 151 and 152 of Chapter VIII of the Bombay Civil Service Rules.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order of suspension pending an inquiry into a criminal charge automatically terminates upon the acquittal of the employee in the criminal proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The order of suspension, which was issued pending a criminal inquiry, should automatically terminate upon the employee's acquittal in those criminal proceedings. (inferred)
respondent_arguments: An acquittal in a criminal proceeding does not automatically lead to the termination of a suspension order, as the government can still proceed with a separate departmental inquiry for misconduct. (inferred)

cases.case_name: R. P. Kapur v. Union of India
cases.principle: To support the legal validity of an order suspending an employee pending an enquiry into their conduct.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A suspension order is not terminated automatically but only by another order of the Government. Until a further order is made terminating the suspension, the employee has no right to be reinstated in service or to the remuneration claimed.
obiter: In a case falling under clause (b) it will not be treated as a period spent on duty unless the revising or appellate authority so direct.
Fundamental Rule 53 contemplates all kinds of suspension.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An order of suspension that is explicitly made "pending further orders" does not automatically terminate upon the acquittal of the employee in a related criminal proceeding. The suspension remains legally valid and in effect until a separate, subsequent order is issued by the government to terminate it, as the government retains the right to conduct a separate departmental inquiry.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of the specific language of the suspension order to determine its duration and conditions for termination.
Distinguishing precedent based on material differences in the facts and the specific rules under which the suspension orders were issued.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's suspension order could not terminate automatically because it was explicitly made "pending further orders", which required a subsequent government order to end it.
The appellant had no right to be reinstated or claim remuneration until a further order was made by the State Government terminating the suspension.

The precedent cited by the appellant, Narayan Prasad Rewany v. State of Orissa, was not applicable because the suspension order in that case did not contain the phrase "pending further orders" and was issued under a different service rule.
why_respondent_won: The specific language of the suspension order, stating it was "pending further orders," meant that the order's termination was not automatic but required a positive action from the government.

The acquittal in the criminal proceeding did not extinguish the government's authority to maintain the suspension, as a separate departmental inquiry into the employee's conduct could still be pursued.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning implicitly supports the policy that an employer (the government) retains the right to conduct its own disciplinary inquiry into an employee's conduct, independent of the outcome of criminal proceedings, which operate under a different standard of proof.
